title: Authentication & Authorization
subtitle: Establish identity, enforce permissions, and contain compromised credentials
objectives: Distinguish authentication, session management, and authorization
Choose between server-side sessions and signed access tokens from revocation and scaling requirements
Enforce permissions at the service that owns the protected resource
Design expiration, rotation, and service-to-service identity without exposing long-lived secrets

exercises.title: Authentication establishes who is making the request
exercises.body: Authentication verifies evidence such as a password, passkey, or identity-provider assertion and binds the successful result to an account. A session then carries that identity across later requests without repeating the primary credential.
exercises.note: The application should store a password verifier produced by a password-hashing function with a unique salt, never the original password.

exercises.prompt: Every API request currently sends the user's password to each backend service. Replace repeated password handling with a revocable server-side session.
choices: Copy the password into every service
Issue a random session ID in a secure cookie
Put the password in a signed token
choiceFeedback: Distributing the primary credential increases the number of systems that can expose it.
A random session ID lets services use an identity reference while the server retains revocation control.
A signature prevents modification but does not make a password safe to distribute.
exercises.beforeStatus: CREDENTIAL EXPOSURE · password reaches 6 services per request
exercises.afterStatus: CREDENTIAL EXPOSURE · password reaches identity service only at sign-in
exercises.result: Later requests carry a revocable identity reference
exercises.why: A high-entropy session identifier reveals no password and maps to server-controlled identity state. Deleting or expiring the session revokes subsequent requests; the cookie also needs Secure, HttpOnly, and an appropriate SameSite policy.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: Every API request currently sends the user's password to each backend service. Replace repeated password handling with a revocable server-side session. Place API, Session store. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Client → API; API → Session store. That topology is the evidence for the answer: A high-entropy session identifier reveals no password and maps to server-controlled identity state. Deleting or expiring the session revokes subsequent requests; the cookie also needs Secure, HttpOnly, and an appropriate SameSite policy.

exercises.prompt: A user has successfully signed in. What should a session prove on the next request?
choices: That the request is associated with an authenticated account under a valid session
That every requested action is permitted
That the device cannot be compromised
exercises.why: A valid session associates the request with an authenticated identity. Authorization still evaluates whether that identity may perform the requested action; authentication does not prove device safety or grant every permission.

exercises.prompt: Match each credential mechanism to the property it supplies.

pairs.right: Verifies a password without storing the original
Opaque reference to server-controlled session state
Carries claims whose modification can be detected

exercises.why: Password hashing protects stored password verifiers, an opaque session ID points to state the server can revoke, and a signed token protects claim integrity. A signature does not encrypt the claims or prove that the presenting device is trustworthy.

exercises.prompt: Which controls reduce session-cookie theft or misuse? Select all that apply.
choices: Send the cookie only over HTTPS
Use a suitable SameSite policy and CSRF defense
Make the session ID predictable so support can reproduce it
exercises.why: Secure transport prevents network exposure, HttpOnly limits script access, and SameSite plus explicit anti-CSRF controls restrict cross-site submission. Session identifiers require enough entropy that an attacker cannot guess another user's value.

exercises.prompt: A banking dashboard must terminate access immediately when support disables an account. Choose the session design emphasis.
exercises.why: Immediate account disablement requires each protected request to consult revocable state or a mechanism with equivalent enforcement. Long-lived self-contained tokens remain valid until expiry unless the system adds a denylist, introspection, or short lifetimes.

exercises.title: Authorization evaluates an action on a resource for an authenticated principal
exercises.body: Authorization combines the authenticated principal, requested action, resource attributes, and policy. The service that owns the resource must enforce the result because it has the authoritative ownership and state needed for the decision.
exercises.note: A user interface may hide forbidden controls for usability, but client-side hiding is not an enforcement boundary.

exercises.prompt: The web app hides the Delete button from viewers, but `DELETE /documents/9` succeeds when called directly. Move enforcement to the protected operation.
choices: Check role and document ownership in the document service
choiceFeedback: An attacker can discover or replay an obfuscated endpoint.
The resource-owning service can reject the operation using authoritative policy and ownership data.
A server cannot rely on controlling tools on the user's device.
exercises.beforeStatus: DIRECT API CALL · viewer deletes document 9
exercises.afterStatus: DIRECT API CALL · 403 Forbidden · document remains
exercises.result: The permission is enforced at the resource boundary
exercises.why: The document service must authorize every protected operation because requests can bypass the web interface. The check should use the authenticated principal and current resource state, then return a non-success response without performing the mutation.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: The web app hides the Delete button from viewers, but `DELETE /documents/9` succeeds when called directly. Move enforcement to the protected operation. Place Document service, Document 9. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Viewer → Document service; Document service → Document 9. That topology is the evidence for the answer: The document service must authorize every protected operation because requests can bypass the web interface. The check should use the authenticated principal and current resource state, then return a non-success response without performing the mutation.

exercises.prompt: Match each authorization model to its decision inputs.

pairs.right: Policy evaluates principal, resource, action, and environment attributes
A resource lists principals or groups and their allowed actions

exercises.why: Role-based access control groups permissions into roles, attribute-based access control evaluates policy over request context, and an access-control list attaches allowed principals or groups to a resource. Systems often combine these models.

exercises.prompt: Complete the authorization path. The gateway authenticates the token; the document service must use current ownership data before returning the document.
exercises.why: The gateway can establish identity, while the document service evaluates the action using current resource ownership and policy. Central authentication does not remove resource-specific authorization from downstream services.

exercises.prompt: A support agent may refund orders only in their assigned region and only below $500. Which facts belong in the authorization decision?
choices: The color of the agent's browser
exercises.why: The policy compares principal attributes with resource and action attributes: assigned region, order region, and refund amount. Unrelated presentation details should not affect the permission decision.

exercises.prompt: A user's role changed from admin to viewer, but an access token still says `role=admin`. What determines how long the old permission can survive?
choices: The token's remaining lifetime and any revocation or introspection mechanism
exercises.why: A self-contained token carries the role snapshot until expiry unless protected services consult current state through introspection, versioning, or revocation. Token lifetime therefore bounds stale authorization when no online check exists.

exercises.title: Short-lived credentials limit exposure; rotation preserves continuity
exercises.body: An access credential should live only as long as its exposure risk permits. A narrowly scoped refresh mechanism can obtain new short-lived access credentials, while rotation invalidates the previously used refresh value and detects replay.
exercises.note: Credential rotation requires overlap or coordinated rollout for legitimate clients; replacing a secret everywhere at one instant is rarely reliable.

exercises.prompt: Show the minimum components and flows that implement this mechanism: Short-lived credentials limit exposure; rotation preserves continuity
exercises.why: An access credential should live only as long as its exposure risk permits. A narrowly scoped refresh mechanism can obtain new short-lived access credentials, while rotation invalidates the previously used refresh value and detects replay. Credential rotation requires overlap or coordinated rollout for legitimate clients; replacing a secret everywhere at one instant is rarely reliable.

exercises.prompt: Build a refresh-token rotation flow after an access token expires.
steps: Client sends the refresh credential to the identity service
Identity service verifies validity, scope, and reuse status
One atomic rotation transaction marks the old refresh credential used and creates its replacement
Identity service returns the new access token and refresh credential
Client replaces the stored credential pair
exercises.why: Rotation treats each refresh credential as single-use. The old-token consumption and replacement creation must be one atomic state transition: two concurrent uses cannot create two successor chains, and a crash cannot consume the old token without recording the replacement. Later reuse can then trigger family revocation or another explicit compromise response.

exercises.prompt: Service A calls Service B with a shared secret embedded in both source repositories. What is the primary operational problem?
choices: Compromise or rotation affects every holder, and the secret is difficult to attribute to one workload
exercises.why: A shared static secret has a broad blast radius, weak workload attribution, and difficult rotation. Workload identity can issue short-lived credentials to a specific service instance and let Service B authorize that principal and scope.

exercises.prompt: Build a service-to-service identity path using short-lived workload credentials.
exercises.why: A workload identity system binds a short-lived credential to Service A's runtime identity. Service B validates the issuer, audience, expiry, and allowed scope instead of trusting a long-lived secret copied across deployments.

exercises.prompt: Which events should invalidate or restrict credentials? Select all that apply.
exercises.why: Account disablement, compromise recovery, and refresh-token replay all change the acceptable identity risk and should revoke or constrain credentials. An unrelated presentation deployment does not alter authentication state.

exercises.prompt: An internal reporting tool contains low-sensitivity data and must keep working through a brief identity-store outage. Choose the access-token emphasis.
exercises.leftLabel: Very short life · frequent online renewal
exercises.why: A moderately longer token lifetime can preserve access during a short identity-service outage, while increasing the window for stale permissions or stolen-token use. The acceptable point follows data sensitivity, revocation requirements, and outage objectives.

exercises.prompt: A document service verifies that a token is valid but never checks whether its subject may access document 42. What is missing?
exercises.why: Authentication establishes who presented the token. Authorization must still evaluate that identity, action, resource, ownership, and policy before returning document 42.
